items.title: George Wein interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: It was before the war and we were trying to be — you know, Duke Ellington.

ctx.x: Isn’t that interesting. You know I have to remind myself, when you talk about some of those tunes you were playing with your first band, they sound old but for you guys, that was the current music of the day, is that right?

Oh yes. We were not playing old music. Old music was Bix Beiderbecke. We were playing Teddy Wilson, Benny Goodman, it was swing. That was the hip music of the day, before bebop. It was before the war and we were trying to be — you know, Duke Ellington. But I was getting into it. © Fiillius Jazz Archive -4-
Did your parents like the direction you took?

items.title: George Wein — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: One day (chuckles) when I was in France with Duke and we were in a beautiful place and he played a concert that night, he had a day off to go to Saint-Tropez.

ctx.x: He was gone for literally … I've got the whole list of the dates. You just develop a knack for how to do those things, and you do it the hard way when you are shipping people around. No

difference with your own band. When you've got a gig in Illinois and you want to fly to that town and it costs a fortune, you fly to Chicago on a cheap fare, rent a car and drive a hundred miles to the gig. I mean, it's a way of economics, of the handling of transportation, and, I mean, I'm trying to think of how I set up that, you know. I had different people in different countries; they would each buy three dates, four dates; another country, another promoter would buy three or four; another government would…
Do you remember the first crazy tour you ever booked?
